refs: Folland, Real Analysis ch. 2 and ch. 7

cards.title: Outline the proof that a finite Borel measure on a metric space is regular (open outer, closed inner).
cards.body:
Show that the family of Borel sets that can be squeezed between a closed and an open set up to $\varepsilon$ is a σ-algebra containing the closed sets.

1. Let $\mathcal{G}$ be the Borel sets $E$ such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there are closed $F\subseteq E\subseteq U$ open with $\mu(U\setminus F)<\varepsilon$.
2. Closed sets are in $\mathcal{G}$: for closed $F$ let $U_k=\{x:d(x,F)<1/k\}$. These are open and decrease to $F$ because $F$ is closed. Since $\mu$ is finite, continuity from above gives $\mu(U_k\setminus F)\to0$.
3. $\mathcal{G}$ is closed under complements: if $F\subseteq E\subseteq U$ then $U^c\subseteq E^c\subseteq F^c$, with $U^c$ closed, $F^c$ open and $F^c\setminus U^c=U\setminus F$.
4. Countable unions: let $E=\bigcup E_j$ with $F_j\subseteq E_j\subseteq U_j$ and $\mu(U_j\setminus F_j)<\varepsilon2^{-j-1}$. Then $U=\bigcup U_j$ is open and $\mu(U\setminus\bigcup F_j)<\varepsilon/2$. By continuity from below, $F=\bigcup_{j\le N}F_j$ (closed) satisfies $\mu(U\setminus F)<\varepsilon$ for large $N$.
5. So $\mathcal{G}$ is a σ-algebra containing the closed sets, hence all Borel sets.

Where the metric is used: step 2, closed sets are $G_\delta$. In a general topological space a closed set need not be a countable intersection of open sets.

refs: Folland, Real Analysis ch. 2 and ch. 7

cards.title: State the **change of variables formula** for Lebesgue integrals on open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
cards.body:
If $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is open and $G:\Omega\to G(\Omega)$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto an open set, then $\int_{G(\Omega)}f\,dm=\int_\Omega(f\circ G)\,|\det DG|\,dm$ for every measurable $f\ge0$ and every $f\in L^1(G(\Omega))$.

Here $\det DG$ is the Jacobian determinant. The factor $|\det DG(x)|$ is the local volume scaling of the linear map $DG(x)$.

Tip: it is enough that $G$ is an injective $C^1$ map with $\det DG\ne0$ everywhere; the inverse function theorem then makes $G$ a diffeomorphism onto an open set. The formula also survives if injectivity or invertibility fails only on a null set, which is how polar coordinates are used.

Watch out: the absolute value of the determinant, not the determinant. If $G$ is not injective the right side counts multiplicity.

cards.title: Outline the proof of the change of variables formula.
cards.body:
Linear case, then a cube-by-cube estimate with the derivative frozen, giving one inequality for all $f\ge0$; applying it to $G^{-1}$ gives equality.

1. Linear $G$: $m(G(E))=|\det G|\,m(E)$.
2. Cube estimate: if $Q\subseteq\Omega$ is a closed cube (sup norm) and $\|DG\|\le M$ on $Q$, the mean value inequality puts $G(Q)$ in a cube of side $M\cdot$side$(Q)$, so $m(G(Q))\le M^nm(Q)$.
3. Freeze the derivative: cut $Q$ into tiny cubes $Q_j$ with centers $y_j$. By uniform continuity of $DG$ on $Q$, $H_j=DG(y_j)^{-1}\circ G$ has $\|DH_j\|\le1+\varepsilon$ on $Q_j$. Then $m(G(Q_j))=|\det DG(y_j)|\,m(H_j(Q_j))\le(1+\varepsilon)^n|\det DG(y_j)|\,m(Q_j)$.
4. Summing and using continuity of $|\det DG|$: $m(G(Q))\le\int_Q|\det DG|$.
5. Every open $U\subseteq\Omega$ is a countable union of non-overlapping dyadic cubes, giving $m(G(U))\le\int_U|\det DG|$. Regularity extends this to Borel sets, then simple functions, then $f\ge0$ by monotone convergence: $\int_{G(\Omega)}f\le\int_\Omega(f\circ G)|\det DG|$.
6. Apply the inequality to $G^{-1}$ and to the function $(f\circ G)|\det DG|$. Since $\det D(G^{-1})(G(x))\cdot\det DG(x)=1$, this gives the reverse inequality. The $L^1$ case follows by splitting.

Key idea: the freezing in step 3 is the same trick as the derivative approximating a function by a linear map, upgraded to volumes.

cards.title: State the **polar coordinates** formula on $\mathbb{R}^n$ ($n\ge2$), where **surface measure** $\sigma$ on $S^{n-1}$ is defined by $\sigma(E)=n\,m(\{rx':0<r\le1,\ x'\in E\})$ for Borel $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$.
cards.body:
For Borel measurable $f\ge0$ (or integrable $f$): $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\,dx=\int_0^\infty\!\!\int_{S^{n-1}}f(rx')\,r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(x')\,dr$.

For a radial function $f(x)=f_0(|x|)$ this reads $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f_0(|x|)\,dx=\sigma(S^{n-1})\int_0^\infty f_0(r)\,r^{n-1}\,dr$.

Why: the map $x\mapsto(|x|,x/|x|)$ carries $m$ on $\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}$ to the product of $r^{n-1}\,dr$ and $\sigma$. The factor $r^{n-1}$ comes from the scaling $m(cE)=c^nm(E)$, and the constant is the definition of $\sigma$.

Check: for $n=2$, $\sigma$ is arc length and $\sigma(S^1)=2\cdot\pi=2\pi$. In general $\sigma(S^{n-1})=n\,m(B)$ for the unit ball $B$.

Watch out: this $\sigma$ is defined through volumes of cones, so no differential geometry is used.

cards.title: What is the volume $\omega_n$ of the unit ball of $\mathbb{R}^n$, in terms of the Gamma function $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty x^{s-1}e^{-x}\,dx$?
cards.body:
$\omega_n=\dfrac{\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma\!\left(\frac n2+1\right)}$

Derivation: $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}e^{-|x|^2}\,dx=\big(\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-t^2}dt\big)^n=\pi^{n/2}$ by Tonelli. In polar coordinates the same integral is $\sigma(S^{n-1})\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r^{n-1}\,dr=\sigma(S^{n-1})\cdot\frac12\Gamma(\frac n2)$ (substitute $s=r^2$). So $\sigma(S^{n-1})=\frac{2\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2)}$, and $\omega_n=\sigma(S^{n-1})/n=\frac{\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2+1)}$ using $\frac n2\Gamma(\frac n2)=\Gamma(\frac n2+1)$.

Checks: $\omega_1=2$, $\omega_2=\pi$, $\omega_3=\frac{4\pi}3$, $\omega_4=\frac{\pi^2}2$.

Watch out: $\omega_n$ is not monotone in $n$. It peaks at $n=5$ ($\omega_5=\frac{8\pi^2}{15}\approx5.26$) and then tends to $0$ faster than any exponential.

cards.title: Compute $\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}e^{-(x^2+xy+y^2)}\,dx\,dy$ exactly.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt3}$

Write $x^2+xy+y^2=v^{\mathsf T}Av$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1\end{pmatrix}$, symmetric positive definite with $\det A=\tfrac34$.

Let $u=A^{1/2}v$, a linear change of variables with $|\det A^{1/2}|=\sqrt{\det A}=\frac{\sqrt3}2$. Then $dv=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\,du$ and the integral is $\frac2{\sqrt3}\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}e^{-|u|^2}\,du=\frac2{\sqrt3}\,\pi=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt3}$.

General formula: $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}e^{-v^{\mathsf T}Av}\,dv=\pi^{n/2}/\sqrt{\det A}$ for positive definite $A$.

Check by completing the square: $x^2+xy+y^2=(x+\frac y2)^2+\frac34y^2$, so the integral is $\sqrt\pi\cdot\sqrt{\frac{4\pi}3}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt3}$.

Watch out: the Jacobian enters inverted. The variable $u$ is the one that is rescaled, so $dv=|\det A^{1/2}|^{-1}du$.

cards.title: For which $a>0$ is $|x|^{-a}$ integrable over $\{|x|<1\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, and for which over $\{|x|>1\}$?
cards.body:
Integrable near $0$ iff $a<n$, and integrable near $\infty$ iff $a>n$; so $|x|^{-a}$ is never integrable on all of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

By polar coordinates, $\int_{|x|<1}|x|^{-a}\,dx=\sigma(S^{n-1})\int_0^1r^{n-1-a}\,dr$, finite iff $n-1-a>-1$, i.e. $a<n$, and then equal to $\frac{\sigma(S^{n-1})}{n-a}$.

Likewise $\int_{|x|>1}|x|^{-a}\,dx=\sigma(S^{n-1})\int_1^\infty r^{n-1-a}\,dr$, finite iff $n-1-a<-1$, i.e. $a>n$, and then equal to $\frac{\sigma(S^{n-1})}{a-n}$.

Tip: the same method decides integrability of $|x|^{-a}(1+|x|)^{-b}$: it needs $a<n$ for the singularity at $0$ and $a+b>n$ at infinity.

Watch out: at $a=n$ both ends diverge logarithmically, which is the borderline case in many qualifying exam problems.

cards.title: Let $\mu$ be a Radon measure on a locally compact Hausdorff space $X$. Show that $C_c(X)$, the compactly supported continuous functions, is dense in $L^1(\mu)$.
cards.body:
Reduce to indicators of sets of finite measure, sandwich $E$ between a compact $K$ and an open $U$ with $\mu(U\setminus K)<\varepsilon$, and insert an Urysohn function $\varphi$ with $\chi_K\le\varphi\le\chi_U$.

1. Simple functions $\sum a_j\chi_{E_j}$ with $\mu(E_j)<\infty$ are dense in $L^1(\mu)$ (simple approximation plus dominated convergence). So it suffices to approximate $\chi_E$ with $\mu(E)<\infty$.
2. Outer regularity gives an open $U_1\supseteq E$ with $\mu(U_1)<\mu(E)+\varepsilon$, so $\mu(U_1\setminus E)<\varepsilon$, and then an open $U_2\supseteq U_1\setminus E$ with $\mu(U_2)<\varepsilon$.
3. Inner regularity on the open set $U_1$ gives a compact $K'\subseteq U_1$ with $\mu(U_1\setminus K')<\varepsilon$. Let $K=K'\setminus U_2$. It is compact, and $K\subseteq U_1\setminus U_2\subseteq E$. Also $\mu(E\setminus K)\le\mu(U_1\setminus K')+\mu(U_2)<2\varepsilon$.
4. The Urysohn lemma for locally compact Hausdorff spaces (apply it in the one-point compactification) gives $\varphi\in C_c(X)$ with $0\le\varphi\le1$, $\varphi=1$ on $K$ and $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq U_1$.
5. $|\chi_E-\varphi|$ vanishes on $K$ and outside $U_1$, and is at most $1$ elsewhere. So $\|\chi_E-\varphi\|_1\le\mu(U_1\setminus K)<2\varepsilon$.

Watch out: both regularity properties are used. Without outer regularity one cannot control $\mu(U\setminus E)$, and without inner regularity one has no compact $K$.
